private two-way chat and audio calls inside the platform
daily check-in: a short mood form visible only to the mentor
full contact history and mood log over time
mentor ratings and verification by sobriety length and user reviews
antiFeatures: unmoderated group chats
gamification and badges
content feeds and motivational quotes
sobriety-1.monetization: User subscription ($15-30/month), 60-70% goes to the mentor, corporate wellness packages sold through HR

sobriety-2.title: Sober Employer
sobriety-2.oneLiner: A B2B tool for HR: anonymous addiction screening, an employee assistance program, and treatment outcome tracking across the workforce
sobriety-2.gap: Employers pay for health insurance and sick days but have no way to see how many employees struggle with alcohol or nicotine addiction, and no way to help them anonymously
sobriety-2.pitch: A company adds the platform as an extension of its health plan or as a standalone employee assistance program. An employee takes an anonymous screening, gets a personal support plan, and can access mentors or therapists. HR sees only aggregated stats and ROI: fewer sick days and lower turnover.
features: anonymous addiction screening for employees using the AUDIT test and similar tools
personal plan with recommendations, exercises, and scheduled therapist sessions
integration with the corporate portal and health insurance card
HR dashboard with aggregated data and no personal identifiers
quarterly report on risk reduction and sick-day savings
antiFeatures: identifying individual employees to HR
mandatory notifications to work email
gamification and leaderboards
sobriety-2.monetization: B2B subscription from $3-8 per employee per month, bundled into corporate health plans or purchased separately by HR

sobriety-3.title: Crisis Button
sobriety-3.oneLiner: A single-purpose app with one job: press it during a craving and get live support within three minutes
sobriety-3.gap: At the sharpest moment of a craving, help is either behind a paywall, broken, or just text that does nothing when emotions are running high
sobriety-3.pitch: You press one button. Within three minutes a on-call mentor or counselor joins a short call. No onboarding, no subscription required before your first contact. You pay only for the minutes you use, the same way you would pay for an ambulance.
features: one large button on the screen that triggers a queue of on-call mentors
voice or text contact with a real mentor within one to three minutes
short grounding exercises while you wait (breathing, sensory anchoring)
crisis log: when it happened, how long it lasted, how it resolved
pay-per-use: charged per minute of call or prepaid minute packs
antiFeatures: monthly subscription before first use
mandatory registration and intake form at install
day counter and progress tracker
sobriety-3.monetization: Per-call pricing ($1-2 per minute) or minute packs ($5 for 5 minutes), insurance companies can pay per enrollment as a health plan add-on

sobriety-4.title: Digital Detox for Teens
sobriety-4.oneLiner: A recovery program for feed-scrolling and vaping addiction aimed at 13-17 year olds, purchased by parents
sobriety-4.gap: Teens are locked out of most sobriety apps by age restrictions, and adult communities shame and push them away
sobriety-4.pitch: A parent pays for a 30-day course for their child. The teen goes through it on their own: daily tasks, video mentors their own age, and a closed community for teenagers only. The parent can see progress without accessing their child's personal entries.
features: sign-in without a card or age verification through a parent account
content and mentors aged 16-22 who have been through it themselves
closed community for teens only with active moderation
daily micro-tasks written in the style and language of teenagers
parent dashboard showing daily completion only, with no personal content
antiFeatures: open chats shared with adults
clinical tone and medical terminology
ad banners and ad-based monetization
sobriety-4.monetization: Parent pays a one-time course fee ($20-40 for 30 days) or a subscription, schools and child psychologists buy group licenses

sobriety-5.title: Sobriety Journal with a Real Therapist
sobriety-5.oneLiner: A daily structured journal for people in remission, paired with a weekly therapist session where the therapist has already read your entries
sobriety-5.gap: Journaling in apps breaks, goes unanswered, and nobody reads what you wrote on your hardest day
sobriety-5.pitch: The user keeps a journal with structured prompts every day. A therapist reads the entries and runs a 30-minute session once a week already knowing the context of the week. The cost is a fraction of private therapy because the therapist does not spend the session asking what happened.
features: daily prompts: a morning intention and an evening reflection
craving log: when it happened, what triggered it, how it went
therapist sees the full entry feed before each session
30-minute video session once a week inside the platform
PDF export of entries for personal records
antiFeatures: AI responses instead of a real therapist
public journal or open community
motivational quotes and content feeds
sobriety-5.monetization: Subscription $50-80/month includes a therapist and unlimited journaling, therapists keep 60% and the platform takes 40%

sobriety-6.title: Gentle Exit from Alcohol
sobriety-6.oneLiner: A medically guided program for cutting back on alcohol, with a drink tracker, a doctor, and a personalized 12-week plan
sobriety-6.gap: People want to drink less, not quit entirely, but every app pushes for complete abstinence and a strict day count
sobriety-6.pitch: You do not have to quit: you set your own goal (two glasses on Friday instead of a bottle every day). An addiction doctor builds a reduction plan, the tracker records what you actually drink, and the algorithm adjusts the plan each week. After 12 weeks you have either hit your goal or you move to the next level.
features: drink tracker with no pressure to quit completely
initial online session with a doctor to set a reduction goal
weekly plan adjustment based on tracker data
neuroscience explanations of what alcohol does to sleep and anxiety
option to switch to full abstinence and a new plan whenever you are ready
antiFeatures: sobriety day counter that resets when you have a drink
moralizing tone and quotes about the harms of alcohol
open community with public confessions
sobriety-6.monetization: 12-week starter package ($60, includes a doctor and tracker), monthly renewal at $20, insurers and employers pay as a prevention program

sobriety-7.title: Recovery School
sobriety-7.oneLiner: A structured 90-day sobriety course with live group sessions, sold as a one-time product instead of a subscription
sobriety-7.gap: People pay for app subscriptions for years but never get the structure or the sense of a completed journey that a finished course provides
sobriety-7.pitch: You buy the 90-day course once and go through it with a cohort of 10-12 people led by a facilitator who is in recovery themselves. Three live video sessions a week, daily assignments, and a journal. After 90 days you get a certificate and the option to become a facilitator for the next cohort.
features: fixed 90-day path with a clear finish line
live group sessions three times a week with a facilitator
daily assignments: journal, exercises, audio
closed group for cohort members only
graduate certificate and a facilitator training program
antiFeatures: open-ended subscription with no finish line
open community of strangers with no shared history
gamification and points
sobriety-7.monetization: One-time course payment ($80-150), corporate bulk purchases through HR, graduates pay $30 for facilitator certification

nutrition-calories-1.title: Diabetes Tracker with Accurate Net Carb Counting
nutrition-calories-1.oneLiner: A nutrition tracker for people with diabetes and insulin users where net carbs are calculated correctly and no manual adjustments are needed
nutrition-calories-1.gap: People with diabetes need accurate tracking of net carbs and sugar, but every general-purpose tracker gets this wrong in ways that can be dangerous: chia seeds show up as 10 net carbs instead of zero, you can't set your own targets manually, and the default setup pushes a high-carb calculation
nutrition-calories-1.pitch: A person with diabetes or someone on keto already pays for test strips, a CGM app subscription, and dietitian consultations. The one thing missing is a tracker that does not lie about a single critical number. This product takes a niche with medical stakes and sells accuracy as the foundation, not an add-on.
features: Accurate net carb calculation accounting for fiber and sugar alcohols with no manual corrections needed
Manual entry of personal target ranges for carbs, sugar, and glycemic index
Glycemic response history displayed alongside the meal log (CGM data integration via file or API)
A verified food database built for diabetic diets with no user-submitted noise
Weekly PDF reports exportable for a doctor or dietitian
antiFeatures: Gamification, streaks, and mascots
Healthy eating tips and a traffic-light good/bad food system
Photo recognition as the primary entry method
nutrition-calories-1.monetization: People with diabetes already pay for CGMs, test strips, and companion apps. A subscription of $4-6 per month or a one-time purchase fits naturally. Dietitians managing diabetic patients pay for access to patient reports.

nutrition-calories-2.title: Dietitian Practice Dashboard with Patient Food Logs
nutrition-calories-2.oneLiner: A platform for practicing dietitians where each patient keeps a food diary and the specialist sees a real-time summary
nutrition-calories-2.gap: A dietitian spends half of every session deciphering messenger photos and handwritten tables from patients instead of analyzing and giving recommendations. Ready-made B2B tools for nutritionists are almost nonexistent
nutrition-calories-2.pitch: A nutritionist manages 20 to 50 patients and receives their food diaries as WhatsApp screenshots. This platform gives each patient a simple logging app and gives the specialist a structured dashboard with nutrient summaries, deviations from the plan, and body measurement history. The money comes from the practice, not from the patient.
features: Simple patient app: barcode scan, search, one-tap repeat of yesterday's meals
Nutritionist dashboard with a patient list, weekly summaries, and deviations from the individual plan
Per-patient goal setting for calories, protein, fat, and carbs
Automatic weekly PDF report sent to the patient
In-app messaging from the specialist to the patient with no external messengers needed
antiFeatures: Algorithmic advice instead of recommendations from a live specialist
Automatic goal-setting without the specialist's input
Gamification and patient leaderboards
nutrition-calories-2.monetization: Nutritionists and dietitians pay for a practice subscription (a plan for 10 patients at around $18/month, for 50 patients around $50/month). Clinics pay a corporate rate for the whole department.

nutrition-calories-3.title: Nutrition Tracker for Personal Trainers
nutrition-calories-3.oneLiner: A tool for fitness trainers that connects a client's nutrition plan to their training load and shows where the client is falling short on protein or carbs
nutrition-calories-3.gap: A trainer assigns workouts and tracks weight and measurements but has no idea why a client is not recovering. Nutrition is tracked separately in another app or not at all. Connecting calorie burn from training to actual intake today is impossible without manual work.
nutrition-calories-3.pitch: A fitness trainer manages 15 to 30 clients and cannot monitor what they eat between sessions. This platform gives clients a simple log focused on protein and recovery macros, and gives the trainer a dashboard showing which clients consistently undereat on training days. It sells to trainers as a professional tool, not a consumer app.
features: Focus on protein, carbs, and meal timing relative to workouts
Trainer dashboard: client list with summaries for training days vs. rest days
Training schedule synced with the food log without double-counting calories
Nutrition plan templates the trainer can send to the whole group in one click
Alert to the trainer when a client has not logged for more than two consecutive days
antiFeatures: Smart burned-calorie estimates from fitness trackers (a source of errors and double-counting)
Exercise technique tips and training programs
A standalone mode without a trainer
nutrition-calories-3.monetization: Trainers and online coaches pay per active client. Gyms and fitness clubs sign corporate contracts covering their entire training staff.

nutrition-calories-4.title: Calorie Tracker for Local Markets Without the Western Database
nutrition-calories-4.oneLiner: A calorie tracking app where the food database is built for a specific market such as India, Turkey, or the Gulf states with real local dishes and familiar measurements
nutrition-calories-4.gap: People outside the US manually create new entries for every home-cooked meal because no global database knows their food. Every log entry means building a new product from scratch and converting from grams to cups and back.
nutrition-calories-4.pitch: Neither MyFitnessPal nor Cronometer invests in databases for India or the Middle East. The economics of a global database always lose to a local one. This product picks one market, builds the database from the ground up with correct gram-based measurements and local dishes, and becomes the default tracker for an audience that global players quietly ignore.
features: A verified database of local foods and dishes with gram-based entry
Barcode scanner covering local brands
Standard measures for the target market (kati, tawook, handful, with numeric equivalents)
Fast logging of home-cooked meals via a favorites list with no searching required
Week starting on Monday, correct time zone, and local-language UI by default
antiFeatures: Trying to cover all markets at once
Smart photo logging as the primary entry method for home-cooked food
Nutrition advice based on Western dietary standards
nutrition-calories-4.monetization: Subscription for advanced micronutrient tracking and export. B2B sales to corporate wellness programs in the local market. White-label licensing for local insurance companies.

nutrition-calories-5.title: Eating Disorder Recovery Food Diary
nutrition-calories-5.oneLiner: A food journal without scores or traffic lights for people in remission from an eating disorder who need to track intake without being triggered
nutrition-calories-5.gap: People recovering from anorexia or bulimia are often recommended to keep a food diary. But every tracker highlights bad food in red, shows sad faces when you exceed a limit, and offers advice from a mascot. These are direct triggers that drive people away or cause relapse.
nutrition-calories-5.pitch: Psychologists and dietitians working with eating disorders recommend structured food journals as part of recovery, but no existing app fits the task. This product removes everything that judges or shames, leaves only honest logging, and delivers the data to a specialist in a standard format. Revenue comes from specialists, not from already vulnerable users.
features: Neutral log with no scores, color codes, or emoji reactions
Option to log meal regularity and timing, not just nutrients
Specialist dashboard with a weekly report on meal structure
No push notifications of the type 'you have not eaten in 4 hours'
Specialist-only mode where the client sees the log but not the final totals, if the specialist sets it that way
antiFeatures: Traffic-light good/bad food ratings
Streaks and pressure to keep a chain going
Nutrition tips and suggestions to swap out a dish
nutrition-calories-5.monetization: Specialists (psychologists, dietitians, rehabilitation centers) pay for a dashboard with access to patient diaries. Clinics pay a corporate rate for their full patient flow.

nutrition-calories-6.title: Nutrition Tracker for Menopause and Hormonal Changes
nutrition-calories-6.oneLiner: A nutrition and body measurement tracker for women in menopause where the micronutrients needed during hormonal changes are built into the main flow
nutrition-calories-6.gap: After 45 a woman stops losing weight with the same formula that worked before and starts monitoring calcium, magnesium, iron, and phytoestrogens. No tracker makes these nutrients visible on the first screen. They are hidden three taps deep or locked behind a paid plan.
nutrition-calories-6.pitch: The market for supplements, programs, and specialists serving women in menopause is large and pays well. People in this age group are used to spending money on their health and are looking for a tool that addresses their specific situation rather than averaging toward a 25-year-old. This product is built around the micronutrients of menopause, body measurements, and clear goals. It sells as a specialized health management tool, not just a calorie counter.
features: First screen shows calcium, magnesium, iron, vitamin D, and phytoestrogens alongside the standard macros
Body measurement dashboard: weight, circumferences, and body fat percentage tracked by month
Food database sortable by the relevant micronutrient content
Option to log how you feel alongside the food log (sleep, hot flashes, energy levels)
Clear nutrient goals with food sources explained without medical jargon
antiFeatures: Gamification and streaks
Automatic nutrition advice from an algorithm instead of a specialist
Weight loss as the only goal
nutrition-calories-6.monetization: Women 45+ already pay for supplements, lab tests, and consultations. A subscription of $5-8 per month fits naturally as part of health spending. Partnerships with calcium and magnesium brands as native integrations.

nutrition-calories-7.title: Corporate Nutrition Program for Employers
nutrition-calories-7.oneLiner: A platform for corporate wellness programs where HR sees aggregated nutrition statistics for the workforce and each employee keeps a personal anonymous diary
nutrition-calories-7.gap: Corporate wellness programs come down to a quarterly lecture and a gym discount. The employer pays for the program but has no idea whether it works. There is no tool that provides an anonymous aggregated picture of the team's nutrition without violating individual privacy.
nutrition-calories-7.pitch: Large employers already spend on corporate health: medical insurance, gym access, mental health support. Adding a nutrition tracker as a tool with measurable outcomes is easier than launching a new program from scratch. An HR manager sees aggregates by department without access to any individual's data, which makes the program acceptable to employees. The contract is signed once a year for the whole company.
features: Simple employee app: barcode scan, search, fast logging
Anonymous aggregated statistics for HR showing the share of employees hitting their protein and fiber targets
Company-wide weekly challenges such as drink more water or add vegetables, with no scoring
Quarterly HR report with trend data by department
No ads, no selling employee data to third parties. This is part of the contract.
antiFeatures: Individual rankings and employee-to-employee comparisons
HR access to any individual's personal data
Gamification with public leaderboards
nutrition-calories-7.monetization: Employers pay per employee (roughly $1-2 per person per month on an annual contract). HR platforms buy it as a white-label module for their corporate portals.

kids-learning-1.title: Reading Without a Paywall
kids-learning-1.oneLiner: A reading program for kids ages 5 to 9 that takes a child from the very first letter to fluent reading, with no payment wall mid-lesson and no ads
kids-learning-1.gap: A child gets hooked on an app, hits a paywall at the third letter, and melts down. The parent pays but has no idea whether it will work, and the method counts guessing as reading

idea.pitch: Parents pay once for the full course from letters to connected reading, not for a subscription they can never cancel. The program tracks real progress: a child cannot move on until the word is read correctly, not guessed on the third try. The course is designed for ages 5 to 9 and covers the full path from the alphabet to reading books independently.
features: Full course with no subscription: one payment, all content unlocked forever
Phonics trainer: the child hears a sound, says it aloud, and the app only accepts clear pronunciation
Parent progress map: which letters and syllables are mastered, how many words read this week
Offline mode: all lessons work without internet, progress syncs when connection returns
PIN-protected profile: the child cannot accidentally open a browser or reset their progress
antiFeatures: No rewards, pets, or room decorations: the child is not chasing tickets instead of lessons
No ads and no pop-up offers inside a lesson
No auto-renewals: payment is one-time, no hidden charges
idea.monetization: Parents of kids ages 5 to 9 already pay for tutors at $10 to $25 per hour or for subscriptions like Reading Eggs at $96 a year. A one-time purchase of the full course at $20 to $35 is easy to understand and removes the fear of surprise charges.

kids-learning-2.title: A Speech Therapist's Pocket Assistant
kids-learning-2.oneLiner: A platform for speech therapists that sends home exercises to children between sessions and shows the specialist exactly how the child practiced
kids-learning-2.gap: A speech therapist sees a child once a week for 40 minutes. Between sessions, the parent is supposed to do exercises at home, but does not know how, forgets, or does them wrong. The specialist gets no visibility into what happened at home and starts from scratch every time

idea.pitch: The therapist builds a set of exercises for the week right in the office, the child completes them at home in a game-like format, and the app writes a report: how many repetitions, where the mistakes were. At the next appointment, the specialist already knows where to start. The therapist pays for a subscription as a professional tool, with no separate charge to parents.
features: Exercise builder for specialists: pick exercises for a specific sound, syllable, or phrase in two minutes
Voice trainer for the child: record pronunciation, play it back, and compare it to a model
Report for the therapist: completion chart, the child's voice recordings over the week, errors by sound
In-app parent chat with the therapist: a quick question without a phone call
Ready-made exercise libraries for dyslalia, rhinolalia, and stuttering, updated by specialists
antiFeatures: No automated diagnosis: the app does not replace a specialist, it makes the specialist more effective
No game rewards or distracting mechanics: the child completes the specific task the therapist assigned
No general app catalog for independent work without a specialist
idea.monetization: Speech therapists in private practice already spend money on flashcard sets, workbooks, and training materials. A subscription at $12 to $25 per month per specialist with unlimited child profiles. Schools and speech therapy centers buy a team plan covering all their practitioners.

kids-learning-3.title: Math for First Grade
kids-learning-3.oneLiner: A structured math course for children ages 6 to 8 aligned to first and second grade curriculum, with a parent report and no side games
kids-learning-3.gap: A 7-year-old can count to 10 in an app but does not understand number composition and cannot solve word problems. Learning games give a sense of progress but do not cover the school curriculum, and the parent finds out only at the test

idea.pitch: The course follows the first and second grade curriculum quarter by quarter: counting, number composition, addition across tens, two-step word problems. Every week the parent gets a summary of what was mastered, what was missed, and what to revisit. No extra mini-games or rewards: the child solves problems and exercises, not collects coins.
features: Program by quarter for first and second grade: the child is ready for class
Two-step word problems with step-by-step walkthrough: the child sees exactly where they went wrong
Weekly parent report: gaps by topic, error trends over time
Weak-spot practice mode: the app focuses the session on topics the child consistently misses
Offline mode for every exercise, no exceptions
antiFeatures: No pets, rewards, or side mini-games: just math
No random topic order: strict sequence following the curriculum
No answer-guessing shortcuts: the child can ask for a walkthrough but cannot brute-force the answer
idea.monetization: Parents of first-graders pay math tutors from $12 per hour. A subscription at $5 to $8 per month or a one-time course purchase at $18 feels like obvious savings. Elementary school teachers assign it as homework: school plan for a whole class.

kids-learning-4.title: Homeschool Planner and Records
kids-learning-4.oneLiner: A tool for homeschooling families that replaces the teacher's gradebook: a year plan, daily schedule, lesson log, and a report for the review committee
kids-learning-4.gap: A family switches to homeschooling and discovers the problem is not content but structure: unclear how to build a year plan, how to prove progress at an evaluation, and how to keep track of what has already been covered

idea.pitch: The parent enters the child's age and country and gets a template curriculum by subject for the school year, broken down by week. Each day they log what was covered and how long it took. At the end of the quarter, the app generates a report for the review board. Sold directly to homeschooling families.
features: Curriculum templates by country and age: Russia, USA, UK, and a flexible custom option
Lesson log: topic, duration, resources used, parent notes
Automatic quarterly report as a table for the committee or a portfolio
Multiple child profiles with separate programs under one account
Reminders and a weekly plan: what is scheduled today, what was postponed
antiFeatures: Does not try to replace textbooks or educational content: only organization and record-keeping
No game layer: this is a tool for the parent, not an app for the child
No social or community features: the family log is private
idea.monetization: Homeschooling families in Russia and the US pay for curriculum materials, courses, and planning tools. A subscription at $6 to $10 per month or a yearly plan at $40. In the US, the homeschooling market covers more than 3 million families with real spending on tools.

kids-learning-5.title: Reading in the Heritage Language
kids-learning-5.oneLiner: A reading course for bilingual children ages 4 to 8 who live in an English-speaking country but whose parents want them to read in their heritage language too
kids-learning-5.gap: A child in the US or Europe learns to read English at school and hears Russian or Hindi at home. The parent looks for an app to teach reading in the heritage language but finds only adapted English apps with poor interface translations and no real pedagogy

idea.pitch: The course starts from zero: the child learns letters, syllables, and words in Russian, Arabic, or Hindi with correct phonetics and a method developed by native-speaking educators. The interface switches entirely to the target language, with no machine translation. The parent picks a language and gets a complete course from the first letter to the first book.
features: Courses in Russian, Arabic, Hindi, and Spanish: each built by native speakers with curriculum specialists
Correct phonetics for each language: real sounds, not transliteration
Two simultaneous language profiles: the child studies both and progress does not get mixed up
Offline mode: lessons work on a plane or in a country with unreliable internet
Parental controls with no browser access
antiFeatures: Does not try to teach both languages at once in one lesson: each course is strictly monolingual
No translation hints in English inside a lesson in another language
No ads and no redirects to YouTube
idea.monetization: Russian-speaking and Arabic-speaking families abroad pay for Saturday schools, tutors, and heritage-language textbooks. A one-time course at $20 to $25 feels cheaper than one tutor session. Diaspora communities spread it by word of mouth.

kids-learning-6.title: Reading for Kids with Dyslexia
kids-learning-6.oneLiner: A specialized reading program for children ages 6 to 12 with dyslexia, built on the Orton-Gillingham method, with tools for the special education teacher
kids-learning-6.gap: A parent of a child with dyslexia buys a standard kids learning app and realizes within a week it does not work: no phoneme analysis, no multisensory approach, no real progress. Specialized programs like Barton cost tens of thousands of rubles and require an in-person specialist

idea.pitch: The program applies the proven Orton-Gillingham method adapted for a screen: multisensory input, step-by-step phoneme mastery, no guessing, spaced repetition. The special education teacher gets a dashboard with each child's progress and ready-made lesson protocols. Sold to schools and speech therapy centers as a specialist tool.
features: Orton-Gillingham method in digital form: phoneme sequence, multisensory input, tracing and sound at the same time
Spaced repetition: weak sounds come back until fully mastered
Specialist dashboard: each child's progress, gap map, exportable parent report
Font and background customization: OpenDyslexic, larger line spacing, reduced contrast
Offline mode for classroom use without Wi-Fi
antiFeatures: Not for a general audience: a narrow program only for children with reading difficulties, not trying to serve everyone
No game distractions: a child with dyslexia needs predictable structure with no surprises
No automatic level progression: the specialist or parent manually unlocks the next level
idea.monetization: Schools and remedial centers already pay for licenses to programs like Lexia Core5 or Read Naturally at $50 to $100 per child per year. A specialist subscription at $30 per month with 20 child profiles. Parents of children with dyslexia pay speech therapists $20 to $40 per session.

kids-learning-7.title: Digital Classroom for Private Tutors
kids-learning-7.oneLiner: A tool for private elementary school tutors: ready-made subject assignments, homework with auto-grading, and parent reports without the admin overhead
kids-learning-7.gap: An elementary school tutor spends an hour preparing assignments, then grades them by hand, and writes a WhatsApp summary to parents. Paid platforms designed for adult EdTech are too complex and expensive, while kids learning apps give the specialist no tools to work with

idea.pitch: The tutor picks a subject, grade, and topic and gets a set of ready-made exercises with difficulty options. The child completes them on their device, the app auto-grades and generates a report for the parent. The tutor spends time teaching, not on paperwork.
features: Exercise bank for Russian, math, and reading for grades 1 to 4, with teaching notes
Lesson builder: the tutor assembles a session from exercises in two minutes
Auto-grading for open and closed answers with error highlighting
Post-session parent report: what was covered, where mistakes were made, what is assigned for homework
Progress log for each student with full session history
antiFeatures: Not a tutor marketplace: does not help find clients, only serves the ones already there
No self-study content for the child to use without the tutor
No social or game mechanics for the student
idea.monetization: A private tutor earns $400 to $1000 per month and clearly values saving an hour a day. A subscription at $12 to $18 per month per tutor with unlimited students. Tutoring centers and children's schools buy a team plan.

time-tracking-1.title: Freelancer Timesheet
time-tracking-1.oneLiner: Track hours and send an invoice to the client right from your phone, no spreadsheets and no manual math
time-tracking-1.gap: A freelancer logs hours in one place and calculates payment in another. Invoices get assembled by hand and full of errors.
time-tracking-1.pitch: A freelancer starts a timer tied to a client and a rate, sets the rate once, and at the end of the period gets a ready-to-send invoice. No spreadsheets, no recalculating by hand. The invoice goes to the client straight from the app in two taps.
features: timer linked to a client and a rate that calculates the total automatically
manual time edits after the fact without losing any existing records
a polished invoice with logo, billing details, and a line-item breakdown by task
multiple clients with different rates for each, including after-hours and rush rates
export to PDF and send by email directly from the app
antiFeatures: no gamification or habit trees: this is a work tool, not a game
no forced sign-up before you can start tracking
no ads and no paywalls on core tracking and export features
time-tracking-1.monetization: Freelancers already pay for accounting services and invoicing tools. Paid tier with unlimited clients and branded invoices, available as a subscription or a one-time purchase.

time-tracking-2.title: Shift Log
time-tracking-2.oneLiner: A digital timesheet for shift workers that calculates overtime, night differentials, and holiday pay
time-tracking-2.gap: A shift worker has no way to verify whether the employer calculated their paycheck correctly. All the formulas are locked away with the payroll department.
time-tracking-2.pitch: A nurse, security guard, or warehouse worker logs their shifts and sees the exact amount owed, factoring in night rates, overtime, and holidays under their country's labor law. If payroll comes in short, the worker has a printed calculation ready for the conversation with management.
features: multiple pay rate types: regular, night, holiday, overtime
net salary calculation with taxes and rates for a specific country
a shift log where you can edit and add entries retroactively
a printable and exportable report for any date range, useful when disputing wages
support for multiple jobs with different rates at each
antiFeatures: no task manager and no Pomodoro mode: just shifts and money
no team features and no employer access to the worker's data
no mandatory cloud sync: data is stored locally on the device
time-tracking-2.monetization: Shift workers already spend money on legal advice and wage disputes. A subscription at 2 to 3 dollars a month, or a one-time purchase for access to advanced pay types and export.

time-tracking-3.title: Agency Time
time-tracking-3.oneLiner: A time tracker for small agencies where each team member logs hours by client and the manager sees a summary and bills in one click
time-tracking-3.gap: In an agency of 3 to 10 people, everyone tracks time their own way. The manager spends hours collecting the data and still sends out invoices based on guesswork.
time-tracking-3.pitch: Each agency employee starts a timer on a client and project from their phone or a widget. The manager sees in real time how many hours have gone into each account and generates an invoice in one click. Disputes over overtime are a thing of the past.
features: a team overview showing who is working on what right now and how many hours this week
hours tied to a client and project with multiple rate options
an automatic consolidated invoice per client for a given period, broken down by team member
export by employee or by client to CSV and PDF
a reminder if a team member forgot to stop or start a timer
antiFeatures: no task management and no kanban board: only time tracking
no corporate roles or org charts: a flat team structure
no complex onboarding: a new team member is ready in 2 minutes
time-tracking-3.monetization: Agencies already pay for project tools and accounting software. A per-active-seat monthly plan with a minimum of 3 seats.

time-tracking-4.title: Parallel Timer
time-tracking-4.oneLiner: A tracker for people juggling multiple activities at once: one timer keeps running when you start a second
time-tracking-4.gap: A person simultaneously listens to a podcast on a walk or switches between two tasks, but every tracker only lets you run one timer at a time.
time-tracking-4.pitch: A researcher, consultant, or developer often works in parallel: a meeting running alongside a side task, studying while training. Parallel Timer lets you run up to five timers at once and see cumulative time for each. At the end of the day the breakdown by category is accurate with no manual recalculation.
features: up to five independent parallel timers running simultaneously
color coding and quick labels for each stream
a daily summary with total time per activity including overlapping intervals
manual editing of any time segment after the fact
a home screen widget to start or pause any stream without opening the app
antiFeatures: no invoicing or payroll calculations: this is purely for tracking
no team features: a single-user app
no task planner: just a stopwatch
time-tracking-4.monetization: Researchers, consultants, and developers already pay for professional time tracking tools. A one-time purchase or an annual subscription for more streams and detailed reports.

time-tracking-5.title: Watch-Only Tracker
time-tracking-5.oneLiner: A time tracker for smartwatches that runs fully standalone without a phone nearby
time-tracking-5.gap: Time tracking on a smartwatch requires the phone to be nearby and unlocked. Without the phone, the watch stops working or loses the recording.
time-tracking-5.pitch: A professional at the gym, on a job site, or in a meeting wants to start a timer on their wrist and forget about the phone. Watch-Only Tracker stores data locally on the watch and syncs to the app at the next connection. The record is never lost even if the phone was off.
features: fully standalone operation on the watch without a constant phone connection
start, pause, and task switch directly from the wrist in one tap
data saved on the watch when there is no phone connection
sync at the next connection with no data loss
daily and weekly summary on the watch without opening the phone
antiFeatures: no complicated setup or permission requests on first launch
no mid-session prompts asking for additional permissions
no lock-in to one watch brand: supports Wear OS and Galaxy Watch
time-tracking-5.monetization: Smartwatch owners pay for apps and already spend money on health and productivity in their ecosystem. A one-time purchase or a subscription, priced like quality watch apps.

time-tracking-6.title: Location Timer
time-tracking-6.oneLiner: A timer that starts and stops automatically based on your location or Wi-Fi connection, no manual tapping required
time-tracking-6.gap: People regularly forget to start or stop the timer when they change work locations. The day's data ends up incomplete or wrong.
time-tracking-6.pitch: A developer or designer arrives at the office or a coworking space and tracking starts on its own. They leave for home and the timer stops. No manual actions at all. The app tracks location changes, logs office time and home time separately, and shows an honest picture of the working week.
features: auto start and stop based on a geo-fence with a configurable radius for each location
Wi-Fi network detection as an alternative to GPS for indoor spaces
multiple geo-fences each linked to different projects and rates
manual correction of records when the automation misfires
a weekly report broken down by location: office, home, client site
antiFeatures: no persistent background drain on the battery: smart geo-fence triggers only at boundary crossings
no corporate employee tracking features: personal use only
no mandatory upload of location data to a server
time-tracking-6.monetization: Remote workers and freelancers with multiple client sites already pay for productivity tools. A subscription or one-time purchase for unlimited geo-fences and Wi-Fi rules.

time-tracking-7.title: Weekly Dashboard
time-tracking-7.oneLiner: A tool for freelancers and professionals that shows the real picture of their working week by project and helps plan the next one
time-tracking-7.gap: A professional working across multiple projects has no clear view of where the time actually went during the week. The subjective feeling rarely matches the reality.
time-tracking-7.pitch: A consultant or product manager tracks time by project throughout the week, then opens the dashboard on Friday and sees the real picture: how many hours went where, where there was overrun, where there was underdelivery. From that data they plan the next week with realistic estimates.
features: a visual weekly time map by project and client with color coding
a plan-vs-actual comparison showing what was estimated and what was spent
automatic detection of overtime and gaps in the week
a next-week template built from patterns in the current week
dashboard export to PDF for reporting to a client or employer
antiFeatures: no Pomodoro and no focus mode: this is analytics, not a productivity motivator
no team leaderboards or competitions
no gamification or rewards: a tool for professionals
time-tracking-7.monetization: Freelancers and consultants pay for analytics and reporting. A subscription with a weekly PDF digest and month-over-month trend comparison.

strength-training-1.title: Trainer Dashboard for Personal Coaches
strength-training-1.oneLiner: A platform where a trainer manages clients with full progression tracking and per-set feedback
strength-training-1.gap: The trainer has no visibility into how a client actually trains between sessions: no shared log, no progression data, no signal when something goes wrong
strength-training-1.pitch: Personal trainers sell programs but have to take their clients' word for it. The trainer dashboard gives the coach a live log of every client session: weights, reps, deviations from the plan, and missed-set alerts. The trainer sees progression and adjusts before the next session, not after.
features: Trainer creates a program and assigns it to a client with personal notes per exercise
Client logs sets at the gym and the trainer sees the log in real time
Automatic weight progression follows the trainer's own scheme, not an algorithm
Alert to the trainer on deviation: missed day, weight below plan, skipped set
In-app chat between trainer and client, threaded to a specific exercise
antiFeatures: No AI planner that rewrites the program without the trainer
No social feed or user comparisons
No public ready-made programs without a trainer behind them
strength-training-1.monetization: Trainers pay a subscription for the client management dashboard. Clients use it free via the trainer's invite. Trainers already pay for Google Sheets, Notion, and specialized apps at 15 to 50 dollars a month.

strength-training-2.title: Marketplace for Strength Programs
strength-training-2.oneLiner: A platform where coaches and athletes sell their real training programs, and buyers get them delivered straight into a tracker
strength-training-2.gap: Someone wants to train on a proven program but finds either a free PDF with no progression logic or an app subscription full of algorithmic noise instead of a real plan from a real coach
strength-training-2.pitch: Coaches and athletes have been sharing programs in PDFs and Google Docs for decades. This marketplace turns any program into a structured tracker with progression built in, and the author sells it as a one-time purchase or subscription. The buyer opens the app and simply trains on the program they trust.
features: Author uploads a program via an editor with all sets, weights, progression scheme, and notes
Buyer pays once or subscribes and gets the program delivered into their tracker
Progression runs automatically according to the logic the author defined, not an algorithm
Author sees analytics: how many people finished the program and where they dropped off
Buyer reviews are tied to specific program weeks, not abstract star ratings
antiFeatures: No algorithmic exercise substitution in place of the author's plan
No program adaptation without the buyer's consent
No platform-made programs, only author-created ones
strength-training-2.monetization: Platform takes a commission on each program sale. Coaches already sell programs through Gumroad and Notion. Here it works as a live tracker, not just a file.

strength-training-3.title: SaaS for Gym Chains
strength-training-3.oneLiner: A tool for gym networks that gives every member a club-issued workout plan and collects data on what people actually do on the floor
strength-training-3.gap: A gym sells memberships but has no idea what members do on the floor, loses them after three months, and does not know why
strength-training-3.pitch: Gym chains spend money on retention and personalization but have no access to real workout data from their members. This platform plugs into the gym's app as a white label or runs standalone: every member gets a plan from the club, logs their sets, and management sees churn risk analytics and equipment usage. Churn drops because a structured plan creates habit and attachment to the location.
features: Club creates programs for members through a trainer panel
Members log workouts and the club sees aggregated data by group and by individual
Automatic churn risk flag: member has not visited in over two weeks
Equipment usage stats: know that the barbell bench is packed during peak hours
White label option: club embeds the tool in its own app with no mention of the platform
antiFeatures: No public social network across clubs
No sale of member data to third parties
No AI advisor for the end user unless the club requests it
strength-training-3.monetization: Club pays per active member per month. Chains already spend on CRM, booking apps, and access control systems. A 10 percent retention lift is worth the added cost.

strength-training-4.title: Verified Exercise Technique Video Library
strength-training-4.oneLiner: A platform of exercise demonstration videos filmed and approved by real coaches, with subscriptions for studios and gyms
strength-training-4.gap: A trainer re-explains technique to every new member in person, then the client watches an outdated animated video in their tracker and does the exercise wrong
strength-training-4.pitch: Every existing tracker uses outdated 3D animations or outright dangerous demonstrations, and users say so explicitly. This platform licenses an up-to-date video library with real coaches on camera for every movement, including close-ups of correct and common wrong form, and sells access to studios, gyms, and tracker developers via API.
features: Real coach on video for each exercise with a breakdown of typical mistakes
Two formats: full demonstration and a 15-second in-gym reminder clip
Coaches and gyms can upload their own videos and monetize them through the platform
API for embedding in trackers and gym apps
Automatic expiration: videos require re-filming or a relevance confirmation after three years
antiFeatures: No 3D animations without a live human on screen
No publishing without review by a coach with verified credentials
No workout tracker, only a technique library
strength-training-4.monetization: Gyms and studios pay a subscription for embedding via QR-code screens. Tracker developers pay for API access. Content creators receive a share of views.

strength-training-5.title: Online Strength Coaching Platform: From Sale to Delivery
strength-training-5.oneLiner: Everything a strength coach needs to run remote clients: payment, plan, log, and feedback in one place
strength-training-5.gap: An online strength coach stitches together five different tools: payment in one place, programs in another, chat in a third, and none of them know anything about the client's training
strength-training-5.pitch: Online strength coaching is growing, but coaches spend half their time on admin: collect payment, send a PDF, wait for a screenshot of results. This platform closes the full loop. The client pays, gets the plan delivered into their tracker, logs sets, and the trainer sees everything and leaves comments. Coaches sell their coaching time, not their admin time.
features: Trainer creates a coaching package with a price and duration and accepts payment right on the platform
Client gets the program in their tracker immediately after payment with no manual transfer
Trainer sees every logged set and can comment directly on it
Automatic reminder to the client if they have not trained in more than three days
Trainer sees a dashboard of all clients with progress and churn risk flags
antiFeatures: No algorithmic programs in place of the trainer
No program marketplace without a live coach behind each one
No social network or trainer rankings
strength-training-5.monetization: Platform takes a percentage of each coaching package sale. Coaches already pay for Calendly, Stripe, Notion, and WhatsApp broadcasts separately.

strength-training-6.title: Corporate Wellness Through Strength Training: B2B for Employers
strength-training-6.oneLiner: Employers buy strength programs for employees with engagement analytics and no access to personal health data
strength-training-6.gap: Corporate wellness offers yoga and meditation, while employees who want the gym get a membership reimbursement with no structure and quit within two months
strength-training-6.pitch: Employers spend money on membership reimbursements but see no outcome and cannot justify the spend. The platform gives each employee a structured strength program matched to their level and goal, while HR sees aggregated engagement without any personal data: the percentage of employees training consistently. Budgeting the program becomes easy to defend.
features: HR creates a company account and sends invites to employees
Employee picks a program matching their level from the platform's curated library
HR sees only aggregated stats: active users per week, average frequency, no names
Gamification for employees without public rankings: personal streaks and personal records
Integration with reimbursement: platform confirms workout activity to the HR system
antiFeatures: No HR access to personal data or specific exercises an employee performs
No forced competition between colleagues
No public employee rankings
strength-training-6.monetization: Employer pays per active employee per month. Corporate wellness budgets at large companies run to hundreds of dollars per employee per year.

strength-training-7.title: Periodization Tool for Competitive Athletes
strength-training-7.oneLiner: A mesocycle and peak planner for powerlifters and strongmen that builds competition prep down to the week
strength-training-7.gap: A competitive athlete builds their periodization in a spreadsheet or in their head because no tracker can plan load backwards from a competition date with peaking and deload built in
strength-training-7.pitch: A powerlifter, strongman, or kettlebell sport athlete competes roughly every quarter. Existing trackers only log the past, they cannot plan the future. This platform takes the competition date and target maxes and builds a mesocycle backwards: when to accumulate volume, when to intensify, when to deload. The log lives in the same system and automatically adjusts future weeks based on actual results.
features: Planner builds a mesocycle backwards from the competition date using the chosen methodology
Load calculator with percentages of max and automatic adjustment based on actual performance
Comparison of the current cycle against previous competition preps
Wellbeing and recovery journal with correlation to training load
Export of the plan for the coach and two-way sync of coach edits with the athlete
antiFeatures: No AI recommendations without a grounded methodology
No beginner programs or general audience content
No social feed
strength-training-7.monetization: Athlete pays an annual subscription. Competitive athletes already pay coaches between 100 and 300 dollars a month, and some run their own periodization. A powerlifting coach pays for a tool that lets them manage several athletes at once.

mood-journaling-1.title: Clinical Mood Tracker for Therapists
mood-journaling-1.oneLiner: A tool the therapist assigns to the patient and reads before each session, not just another personal diary
mood-journaling-1.gap: Therapists recommend an app, patients install it, and the therapist never sees the data. The connection is one-way and incomplete.
mood-journaling-1.pitch: The therapist signs up, creates a workspace, and invites patients. The patient logs daily check-ins with emotions, notes, and physical sensations. Before each session the therapist opens a summary: weekly patterns, the sharpest moments, day-by-day mood trends. The clinic or private practitioner pays. The patient uses it for free.
features: Therapist workspace: patient list with permission-gated access to their data
Weekly pre-session summary: patterns, peaks, and triggers
Rich emotion vocabulary with definitions and the ability to add custom emotions
Body scan: the patient marks where in the body a feeling is located
PDF report export for medical records or supervision
antiFeatures: Tips and exercises shown after check-in. The therapist, not an algorithm, unpacks what happened with the patient.
Gamification and streaks. This is a clinical tool, not a fitness tracker.
AI analysis of journal entries. Entries are read by the live therapist.
mood-journaling-1.monetization: Private-practice therapists already pay for telehealth platforms and assessment tools (PHQ-9, GAD-7). A subscription at $15-30 per month per clinician for unlimited patients.

mood-journaling-2.title: Mood Tracker for People with Bipolar Disorder
mood-journaling-2.oneLiner: A specialized journal for tracking phases and triggers in bipolar disorder, built together with psychiatrists
mood-journaling-2.gap: People with bipolar need more than a mood diary. They need a phase-monitoring tool covering mania, depression, and mixed states. No mainstream app offers this.
mood-journaling-2.pitch: The product is built around one condition: a scale from deep depression to mania (not just sad or happy), daily sleep and energy tracking as early-warning markers, and emergency contacts triggered by signs of an episode. Users can see when their last manic episode started and which triggers preceded it. The psychiatrist sees the same data in their own dashboard and can adjust treatment without waiting for the next appointment.
features: Mood scale from -5 to +5 with clinical descriptions at each level
Daily tracking of sleep, energy, and concentration as phase-shift markers
Automatic alert when a pattern matches what preceded a past episode
Medication log: what was taken, what was skipped, and side effects
Psychiatrist dashboard with access to patient data and a PDF for medical records
antiFeatures: Meditation tips and positive-thinking exercises. This is a clinical tool.
Streaks and points. Pressuring a patient during a depressive phase is counterproductive.
A general vocabulary of 150 emotions. A clinical scale is needed, not a poetic list.
mood-journaling-2.monetization: People managing a chronic illness pay for management tools for years. A subscription at $7-10 per month or $50 per year. Psychiatrists pay for a dashboard covering multiple patients.

mood-journaling-3.title: CBT Journal with Automatic Thought Analysis
mood-journaling-3.oneLiner: A paid journal built on cognitive behavioral therapy protocol. Real CBT worksheets, not internet self-help tips.
mood-journaling-3.gap: CBT requires written exercises between sessions: ABC diary, thought traps, belief challenging. No mainstream app offers this as a structured tool.
mood-journaling-3.pitch: The app implements standard CBT techniques as interactive worksheets: describe the situation, write down the automatic thought, pick a cognitive distortion from a list, write an alternative thought. The therapist can review the patient's completed worksheets before a session and work with live material rather than reconstructing events from memory. The product is sold through psychotherapy communities.
features: Structured ABC diary: activating event, belief, consequence
Library of cognitive distortions with examples to choose from
Challenging technique: five Socratic questions applied to an automatic thought
Weekly distortion frequency tracking to see which thinking traps come up most
Therapist mode: access to patient worksheets with comments before the session
antiFeatures: Meditations and breathing exercises. Other apps handle those.
AI interpretation of thoughts. Analysis is done by a trained therapist, not an algorithm.
Game mechanics and streaks. CBT is work, not a game.
mood-journaling-3.monetization: People in therapy already spend $40-100 per session. A between-session tool at $5-8 per month is an obvious added value. Therapists pay for a dashboard with access to patient materials.

mood-journaling-4.title: Emotion Tracker for People with ADHD and Autism
mood-journaling-4.oneLiner: A minimal check-in tool designed around the cognitive needs of neurodivergent people. No tutorials, no ads, no overload.
mood-journaling-4.gap: Neurodivergent people name their diagnosis directly and look for a tool that fits how they perceive things. Mainstream apps are cluttered and break exactly the focus they are already struggling to hold.
mood-journaling-4.pitch: The product starts with one screen: an emotion wheel, one tap, the entry is saved. No tutorial on first launch, no notifications pushing a subscription upgrade, no transition animations. For people with alexithymia there is an expanded vocabulary with body cues ("what happens in your body when you feel this"). Monetization runs through psychologists and psychiatrists who work with ADHD and ASD.
features: One-tap check-in with no intermediate screens
Expanded vocabulary with body cues for people with alexithymia
Ability to add a custom emotion that is not in the default list
Configurable quiet reminders with no distracting banners
Simple analytics: what you felt most during the past week
antiFeatures: Mandatory onboarding. The person must be able to start immediately.
Upgrade notifications and promotional banners in the entry feed
Complex tab navigation. One flow, one screen.
mood-journaling-4.monetization: ADHD and ASD specialists pay for tools to use with patients. Parents of autistic children pay for things that actually work. A subscription at $4-7 per month plus a clinician license.

mood-journaling-5.title: Mood Journal for Shift Workers and Night Owls
mood-journaling-5.oneLiner: A tracker where "day" follows your schedule, not midnight on the clock
mood-journaling-5.gap: Nurses, security guards, night-shift workers, and night owls do not live by midnight. The rigid calendar day in mainstream apps breaks their logging logic and makes the tool useless.
mood-journaling-5.pitch: The one basic setting that none of the market leaders have implemented: a custom start and end time for the user's own day. Around that sits a simple mood journal with multiple check-ins per day, pattern statistics, and low-friction reminders. The main sales channel is corporate wellness programs at shift-work companies and hospitals.
features: Configurable day start and end time down to the hour
Multiple check-ins within the user's own day without a reset at an inconvenient moment
Shift-aware statistics: which shifts affect mood the most
Reminders tied to the shift schedule rather than fixed clock times
Simple export for corporate HR reports
antiFeatures: Complex emotional therapy. This is a monitoring tool, not psychotherapy.
Sync with a shared calendar. A shift worker has no concept of Mondays and Fridays.
Social features and comparison with other users
mood-journaling-5.monetization: B2B: corporate employee assistance programs (EAP) at hospitals, factories, and security services already pay for employee wellbeing tools. A per-seat team license at $2-6 per person per month.

mood-journaling-6.title: Somatic Tracker: Where Emotions Live in the Body
mood-journaling-6.oneLiner: An app where you mark not just what you feel but where in your body you feel it. Built for somatic therapy and chronic pain work.
mood-journaling-6.gap: Body scan is one of the most requested features among users referred by therapists. No app implements it properly: only iOS, only one app, only as a secondary feature.
mood-journaling-6.pitch: After a check-in, the user opens a body silhouette and marks where exactly the feeling sits. Tension in the chest, heaviness in the stomach, tight shoulders. Over time a somatic map builds up: which emotions tend to live where for this particular person. The target audience is people working with somatic therapists, those practicing mindfulness yoga, and people with chronic pain where psychosomatic and emotional experience are tightly linked.
features: Interactive body silhouette for marking sensation zones
Linked entry: emotion plus body zone plus intensity
Somatic map over a period showing where tension tends to go
Chronic pain support: pain zone tracked as a separate metric
Export for somatic therapist or osteopath
antiFeatures: Cognitive therapy and thought analysis. That is a different tool for a different modality.
A complex vocabulary of 150 emotions. Here the sensation matters, not the label.
Gamification and streaks. Body work calls for a gentle, low-pressure approach.
mood-journaling-6.monetization: Somatic therapists, osteopaths, and chronic pain specialists pay for between-session monitoring tools. A user subscription at $6-10 per month. A clinician license at $25-50 per month.

mood-journaling-7.title: Personal Archive: A Journal Without AI, Built to Last 10 Years
mood-journaling-7.oneLiner: A secure personal journal for people who want to keep entries for years without the risk of losing them and without an algorithm reading them
mood-journaling-7.gap: People keep mood journals for six years and experience data loss as a personal blow. No app focuses on long-term archive integrity and an explicit AI-free promise as a differentiator.
mood-journaling-7.pitch: The product is positioned as "the journal you will still have in 20 years." Local storage with an option for an encrypted cloud backup that only the user can open. An explicit, public commitment to never running AI analysis on entries. The core buyer is someone who already lost their archive when switching phones and trusts no one anymore.
features: Encrypted archive with a key known only to the user
Cloud backup via the user's own encryption key
Migration from popular apps: Daylio, Day One, How We Feel
Free-form diary and mood tracker in a single flow
Clear policy: no entry is ever read by the server
antiFeatures: AI analysis, summaries, and advice based on journal entries
Social features and sharing moods with others
A subscription that expires and locks access to the archive. One-time purchase or lifetime license only.
mood-journaling-7.monetization: A one-time purchase at $15-25 or a lifetime license at $50. People who have already lost four years of entries pay for reliability without hesitation.

reading-tracker-1.title: Streak Club
reading-tracker-1.oneLiner: A subscription that protects your reading streak: built-in insurance against missed days plus a weekly live accountability group
reading-tracker-1.gap: Readers get emotionally attached to 700-day streaks, but a single bug or missed day resets everything. No service sells continuity and human support as the product itself.
reading-tracker-1.pitch: Streak Club sells not a tracker but a reading continuity subscription: streak insurance (one skipped day per month does not reset the counter), a weekly video call with a group of 10-15 readers, and a personal curator who checks in if you go dark. Paying readers already understand the value of a habit and are afraid to lose it. This is not a feature, it is a service product with a live human layer that no app can copy with a button.
features: Streak with a one-miss-per-month grace period and a transparent history log
Weekly group video call with 10-15 members and a dedicated curator
Personal message from the curator if you miss two days in a row
Shared group dashboard showing everyone's progress and longest streak
Monthly certificate report tracking your habit growth over time
antiFeatures: Algorithm or AI book recommendations
Public social feed open to all
ISBN scanner and shelf cataloging
reading-tracker-1.monetization: Subscription at $4-7 per month. The audience already pays for language clubs, fitness groups, and online coaching in the same format.

reading-tracker-2.title: Family Reading Log
reading-tracker-2.oneLiner: One account for the whole family: kids and parents log reading together, and a shared book counts for everyone at once
reading-tracker-2.gap: Parents read aloud to their kids, but no tracker lets them log one book for multiple people at once. Switching between child profiles breaks down and library challenges do not sync.
reading-tracker-2.pitch: A product for families with children aged 5-12 where read-alouds and independent reading are tracked in one place. A single tap logs a book to the parent and both kids at the same time. Monetization comes from selling family subscriptions to libraries and schools running reading marathons: they pay in bulk for whole-class participation, and prizes (pizza, stickers) are triggered automatically from tracker data.
features: Family profile with up to 6 members, each with their own shelf and streak
Log one book to multiple members in a single tap
Child view with no numbers or stats, just stars and a streak
Integration with library and school reading marathon challenges
Automatic notification to the challenge organizer when a goal is reached
antiFeatures: Social feed and public profiles
AI-driven recommendations
Goodreads import and complex settings
reading-tracker-2.monetization: Family subscription at $3-4 per month. Bulk licenses for libraries and schools for the duration of a reading season. Libraries already pay for reader engagement programs.

reading-tracker-3.title: Goodreads Migration Service
reading-tracker-3.oneLiner: A paid service that moves your entire reading history out of Goodreads into any tracker in 15 minutes with nothing lost
reading-tracker-3.gap: Readers want to leave Goodreads (ads, Amazon, product decline) but years of book history keep them locked in. Every migration attempt breaks: rate limits, missing menus, shelves that vanish.
reading-tracker-3.pitch: A paid service that takes a Goodreads CSV export and cleanly delivers all your books into the tracker of your choice, with shelves, dates, ratings, and reviews intact, in 15 minutes and with no manual work. An extra monetization layer is an annual plan where the service keeps a current backup of your data in a safe place no matter which app lives and which one dies.
features: Parses Goodreads export while preserving shelves, dates, and ratings
Delivers to StoryGraph, Hardcover, Bookwyrm, and local JSON
Deduplicates different editions of the same book during transfer
Archives your reading history to the cloud once a year
Notifies you if your source app stops working
antiFeatures: Its own tracker or reading shelf
Recommendations and discovery algorithms
Social features
reading-tracker-3.monetization: One-time migration fee of $3-6. Annual backup subscription at $2-3 per year. An audience with 10 years of reading history is clearly willing to pay to keep it safe.

reading-tracker-4.title: Widget Tracker
reading-tracker-4.oneLiner: Log your reading directly from the home screen, no app launch required
reading-tracker-4.gap: Readers want to mark a session in one tap, but every existing tracker requires opening the app, going through 3-5 screens, and remembering how many minutes you read. Widgets are either absent or broken.
reading-tracker-4.pitch: A product that lives entirely on the phone home screen: a widget with a single button. Tap it, pick a book, mark your page. Three seconds. Done. After a month you have a clean reading session history built up with zero app launches. It monetizes as a utility with a one-time purchase, the kind people pay for without thinking twice because the alternative is opening three screens every day.
features: 2x2 and 4x2 widget with a Log Reading button right on the home screen
Quick selection from your last three books without searching
Page or percentage entry as a single number
Weekly session stats delivered as a notification
CSV export and sync with StoryGraph or Goodreads
antiFeatures: Session timer as a required field
Social feed and others' profiles
Full book catalog and search
reading-tracker-4.monetization: One-time app purchase at $2-5. Readers already buy utility apps without subscriptions. The widget-tracker category converts well into a paid one-time purchase.

reading-tracker-5.title: Ethical Audiobook Service
reading-tracker-5.oneLiner: Audiobook subscription where every purchase goes to a local independent bookstore
reading-tracker-5.gap: A large share of readers want to listen to audiobooks but are ideologically opposed to Audible because of Amazon. Existing ethical alternatives only operate in the US. Paying customers in Europe are not served.
reading-tracker-5.pitch: An audiobook library by subscription where every purchase is shared with an independent bookstore of the listener's choice. DRM-free files that stay with the buyer forever, plus a built-in progress tracker that counts narrators alongside authors in your stats. The paying audience already exists: these are people spending money on Libro.fm and describing it as a million times better than giving money to Bezos.
features: Audiobook catalog with permanent DRM-free downloads
Choose a local bookstore to receive a share of every purchase
Built-in tracker counting books, narrators, and hours
Most-listened-to narrator stat on par with most-read author
Unified reading dashboard covering print, digital, and audio in one place
antiFeatures: DRM and device lock-in
Algorithmic recommendations with no explanation
Ads and promoted titles in the feed
reading-tracker-5.monetization: Subscription at $6-10 per month or per-book purchase. Ethical consumption audience pays for values. Validated by real paying Libro.fm users.

reading-tracker-6.title: Bookshelf as an Asset
reading-tracker-6.oneLiner: A catalog of your home library: what you own, what you have read, and what you no longer need to buy
reading-tracker-6.gap: People with large physical libraries buy the same book twice because they cannot remember if they already own it. No dedicated product exists for managing physical ownership: every tracker conflates what you have with what you want to read.
reading-tracker-6.pitch: An app for cataloging your home library: scan a barcode or type a title and the book lands under Owned, separate from your wish list. At a bookstore you open the app and instantly see whether that book is already on your shelf. It monetizes as a utility with a one-time purchase because an audience with hundreds of books clearly values organization and pays for tools that provide it.
features: Clear four-way split: On My Shelf, Want to Read, Currently Reading, and Finished
Quick in-store check to see if a book is already in your collection
ISBN scanner with title-search fallback for older editions
Physical location tracking: section, shelf, and slot number
PDF and CSV export of your full catalog for backup or moving
antiFeatures: Social feed and comparisons with other readers
Recommendations and book discovery algorithms
Mandatory sign-up to use the core features
reading-tracker-6.monetization: One-time app purchase at $4-6. Collector and organizer audiences pay for utilities without a subscription. Confirmed by direct requests in reviews.

reading-tracker-7.title: Book Club for Teams
reading-tracker-7.oneLiner: A private club for professional readers: a shared team shelf, synchronized reading schedules, and chapter-by-chapter discussion
reading-tracker-7.gap: Corporate reading already happens (team book clubs, required reading for managers) but there is no tool built for it. Fable and Goodreads are made for consumer reading and have no space for team dynamics or structured discussion.
reading-tracker-7.pitch: A closed product for teams of 5-50 people: a leader picks the book of the month, sets chapter deadlines, each team member logs their progress and leaves notes. Once a week the tool automatically compiles a digest of the team's observations from the chapters they finished. Companies already pay for corporate learning. This is the same budget in a different format.
features: Team workspace with a book of the month and a chapter-by-chapter schedule
Each member's progress visible to the admin
Chapter notes: everyone writes a thought and the digest assembles automatically
Reminders with the next chapter deadline
HR report showing participation, reading pace, and discussion activity
antiFeatures: Public profiles and open feed
Algorithm-driven recommendations
Consumer design with memes and pet photos in the feed
reading-tracker-7.monetization: Team subscription at $18-35 per month for 10 seats. Companies pay from learning and development budgets. One corporate client covers dozens of consumer subscriptions.

ai-chat-assistants-1.title: The Editor That Stays in Its Lane
ai-chat-assistants-1.oneLiner: An AI editor for writers and screenwriters that fixes only what you ask it to fix and never rewrites your voice
ai-chat-assistants-1.gap: Writers hand over a draft for proofreading and the assistant rewrites it in its own words. Trust in the tool collapses after the very first unsolicited edit.
ai-chat-assistants-1.pitch: Writers, screenwriters, journalists, and authors pay for an editor, not a co-author. The tool accepts a mode (proofreading, punctuation, style, or structure) and works strictly within it, leaving everything else untouched. Every change is highlighted with an explanation, and rolling it back takes one click.
features: Editing modes: spelling, punctuation, style, and structure can be turned on one at a time
Every change is highlighted and explained, and each one can be accepted or reverted individually
Locked zones: fragments the assistant never touches under any circumstances
Full document version history with a diff for every revision
A change meter that shows the percentage of words altered and warns you if it exceeds the threshold you set
antiFeatures: Does not generate text from scratch, only works with what the author sends
Does not suggest improvements outside the selected mode
Does not store drafts in the cloud without explicit user consent
ai-chat-assistants-1.monetization: Writers and screenwriters already pay for human editors and proofreaders. Subscription 800-1500 RUB per month. B2B for publishing houses and editorial teams.

ai-chat-assistants-2.title: The Assistant With a Memory
ai-chat-assistants-2.oneLiner: An AI assistant for lawyers and freelancers that remembers every case, document, and client without mixing up context
ai-chat-assistants-2.gap: Lawyers and self-employed professionals juggle dozens of cases at once. General-purpose assistants forget context between sessions and blend details from different clients.
ai-chat-assistants-2.pitch: Each client or case gets its own workspace with persistent memory: documents, agreements, deadlines, correspondence. The assistant knows what happened last week, never asks again, and never crosses cases. For small businesses and solo lawyers without a big office, it replaces a human assistant at a fraction of the cost.
features: Isolated workspaces for each client or case
Persistent memory within each workspace: documents, dates, and agreements
Upload folders and multiple files at once instead of one at a time
A case timeline the assistant keeps up to date automatically
Templates for routine tasks: demand letters, contracts, client reminders
antiFeatures: Does not give legal advice on its own, only helps you work with documents
Does not sync data across client workspaces without an explicit action by the user
Does not connect to third-party CRMs without configuration
ai-chat-assistants-2.monetization: Small businesses and solo lawyers already pay for CRMs and legal software. Subscription 2000-4000 RUB per month. Higher B2B price point for team sales.

ai-chat-assistants-3.title: Every Claim Has a Source
ai-chat-assistants-3.oneLiner: A research assistant for analysts and journalists where every statement comes with a link to a primary source
ai-chat-assistants-3.gap: An analyst cannot use the assistant's output in a report or article because there is no way to tell whether a claim is true or a confident fabrication.
ai-chat-assistants-3.pitch: Every fact in the answer has a citation. No source means no claim. Journalists, analysts, and researchers can finally bring AI into their workflow without manually verifying every line. For newsrooms and analytics teams this is a B2B subscription.
features: Every fact in the answer has a clickable link to its source
A confidence level next to each claim: verified, disputed, or unconfirmed
Deep search mode: scans multiple sources and reconciles contradictions
Export to a formatted report with citations in the style you need (APA, GOST, house style)
A source conflict flag that warns you when two authoritative sources disagree
antiFeatures: Does not answer questions when no sources are found. An honest refusal beats a confident lie.
Does not handle creative or entertainment tasks
Does not summarize without sources: no citation means no claim
ai-chat-assistants-3.monetization: Newsrooms, analytics firms, consultancies, and academic users already pay for databases and media monitoring. Subscription from 3000 RUB per month. B2B teams of five or more people.

ai-chat-assistants-4.title: Support Without Judgment
ai-chat-assistants-4.oneLiner: An AI companion for people with chronic illness and their caregivers that helps navigate the daily reality of illness without stigma or waiting rooms
ai-chat-assistants-4.gap: A person living with a chronic illness or dementia faces new questions every single day. Their doctor is unreachable between appointments, and family members do not always understand or have the energy.
ai-chat-assistants-4.pitch: A constant companion that remembers the user's medical history, never passes judgment, explains things in plain language, and helps them remember medications and upcoming appointments. For older adults and their caregivers this genuinely offloads a meaningful share of the daily burden. The business is built on B2B partnerships with pharma companies and insurers.
features: Persistent memory: medical history, medications, and dosing schedules
Reminders for medications and doctor visits
Plain-language explanations of medical terms without fear-mongering
Caregiver mode: gives the caregiver a summary of the person in their care and sends them notifications
A symptom journal with trends to share at the next appointment
antiFeatures: Does not make diagnoses and does not replace a doctor. Always refers the user to a specialist for medical questions.
Does not operate as an emergency service. In a life-threatening situation it immediately provides emergency contact numbers.
Does not share data with third parties without explicit user consent
